### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, A20's observed outgoing transitions went about 40 in 100 to A30, 33 to A31 and 28 to A36; in the later window, about 99 in 100 go to A22, with A30, A31 and A36 almost never its successor. [DIR001]
- A20 and A22 also became adjacent: the pair sat four steps apart in the earlier window but one step apart in about 99 in 100 of the later cases. [LAG001]
- A21 moved the other way: earlier, all of its observed outgoing transitions went to A25, one step away; in the later window they spread about 36 in 100 to A30, 33 to A31 and 31 to A36, and A25 now appears about four steps after A21 rather than next to it. [DIR002, LAG004]
- The exits of the A30/A31/A36 group changed accordingly: earlier, A30, A31 and A36 each led to A22 in roughly 28–38 in 100 of their outgoing transitions (otherwise to one another); in the later window, A22 is almost never their successor (about 0.5 in 100) while A25 appears at about 30–36 in 100. [DIR003, DIR004, DIR005]
- The order between the two groups reversed: earlier, A30, A31 and A36 each came before A21 and before A22 in essentially every trace (100 in 100); in the later window, A21 and A22 each come before A30, A31 and A36 in about 99 in 100, while the activities still co-occur in every trace. [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006]
- Event positions shifted consistently: A21's mean position moved from about 0.62 to 0.53 of the trace and A22's from about 0.47 to 0.38, while A30, A31 and A36 moved from about 0.41 to about 0.59. [POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005]
- The earlier close pairs A20→A31, A20→A36, A31→A22 and A36→A22, present in all 200 earlier traces, occur in only 2 of 200 later traces, though this rests on very few later observations. [LAG002, LAG003, LAG005, LAG006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the group A30, A31, A36 and the segment containing A22 and A21 exchanged their order: in the earlier window the flow ran from A20 into A30/A31/A36, which exited towards A22, with A21 later and immediately followed by A25, whereas in the later window A20 leads directly to A22, A21 follows and now feeds A30/A31/A36, which exit to A25. The reversal is shown directly by six activity pairs whose order flipped from 100 in 100 one way to about 99 in 100 the other with co-occurrence unchanged, and it agrees with the successor changes at A20 and A21, the changed exits of A30/A31/A36, the adjacency changes (A20–A22 now one step apart, A21–A25 four steps apart) and the position shifts; every involved activity appears in all 200 traces of both windows, and 22 control-flow items qualified against roughly 0.28 expected without change, far beyond what a stable process produces. [DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, DIR004, DIR005, LAG001, LAG004, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006]

Limitations: positions are event positions rather than clock times, four lag items rest on only 2 later-window observations, and activities between A22 and A21 are not covered, so the exact boundaries of the exchanged segments are inferred. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a switch in dominance between two pre-existing variants with opposite segment order rather than a relocation of the block itself; with the later order present in 0 of 200 earlier traces, such a variant would have been invisible in the earlier window. [LAG002, LAG003, LAG005, LAG006, POS001, REL001]
